readerTitle: Your CEO wants a price for a pallet maker by Friday
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (대형 물류회사 전략팀이 팔레트 제조사 인수 가격을 정함) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업의 가치는 정답 하나가 아니라 '어떤 현금, 어떤 위험, 언제 받는 돈'이라는 판단의 연쇄이고, 각 판단을 적어 두어야 협상에서 지킬 선이 생긴다.
misconception: 중개인이 보여준 이익에 업계 평균 배수를 곱하면 회사 가치가 나온다. 총액이 더 큰 지불 조건이 항상 더 비싸다.

sources.text: 기업가치 평가의 표준 개념 (현금흐름, 배수, 현재가치, 할인율)

factChecks.note: 세 가지 시나리오 가치($6M / $5M / $3M)는 계산이 아닌 설명용 가정치입니다. 카드에도 'sketches'로 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Your CEO wants a price for a pallet maker by Friday
body: You work on the strategy team of a large logistics company. Your CEO wants to buy a family-owned pallet and crate maker that supplies your warehouses.
The owner is retiring. Her broker has sent a glossy summary. Your job: tell the board what the business is worth, and what to pay. Four calls stand between you and that number.

image.label: A small pallet factory with a price tag hanging from its roof
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나무 팔레트가 쌓인 작은 공장 지붕에 빈 가격표가 매달려 있고, 앞에서 회사원 한 명이 노트북과 계산기를 들고 고민하는 모습. 실제 기업 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which yearly number do you start from?
body: The broker's summary shows **$1.5M a year** in profit. But it's counted before equipment costs. Saws, nailing lines and forklifts wear out, and the owner spends about $300K a year replacing them.

options.text: $1.5M, the figure in the broker's summary
options.feedback: It's the biggest number, so the price looks justified. But as the owner you'd have to spend $300K a year just to keep the plant running, so that money is never really yours.

options.text: $1.2M, the cash left after the equipment the plant needs
options.feedback: You value what the business actually hands its owner each year. The price is lower, but it's built on money you can spend.

options.text: The average profit of the last three years
options.feedback: Averaging smooths out one lucky year, which is sensible. But it still counts the $300K the machines will swallow.

cards.title: Say you chose $1.2M. Now pick a multiple.
body: The broker says similar pallet makers sold for about **6 times** their yearly cash. But one retail chain buys 45% of everything this plant makes, and its contract ends next year.

options.feedback: You pay as if this cash were as safe as the comparable firms' cash. If the chain leaves, you've overpaid by millions.

options.text: A lower multiple for the extra risk, say 4.5 times: $5.4M
options.feedback: Riskier cash is worth less, and a multiple is just a shortcut for risk and growth. You price in the chain without assuming the worst.

options.text: 6 times, but only on cash from other customers: about $3.96M
options.feedback: Very safe for you. But it treats losing the chain as certain, and a buyer who prices the risk more fairly will likely win the deal.

cards.title: Say you chose $5.4M. Now the owner offers two ways to pay.
body: Option one: $5.4M today. Option two: $1.3M a year for five years, **$6.5M in total**.
Your company expects a 10% yearly return on any money it spends.

image.label: A timeline: one $5.4M payment vs five $1.3M payments
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 두 줄. 위쪽 줄은 '오늘'에 큰 동전 더미 하나 ($5.4M). 아래쪽 줄은 1~5년차에 작은 동전 더미 다섯 개 ($1.3M씩). 오른쪽으로 갈수록 동전이 조금씩 옅어지게 표현.

options.text: Pay $5.4M today to keep it simple
options.feedback: Clean, and you owe the seller nothing later. But in today's money it costs about $470K more than the installments.
At 10%, five payments of $1.3M are worth about $4.93M today. The bigger total is the cheaper deal, because most of it is paid later.

options.text: Propose a split: $3M now, $3M next year
options.feedback: It sounds like a compromise, but it's worth about $5.73M today. That's more than paying cash now.

cards.title: Say you took the installments. The CFO wants one slide for the board.
body: Your team sketches three cases. The chain renews: about $6M. It renews at lower prices: about $5M. It leaves: about $3M.

options.feedback: Easy to read. But it hides how much rides on the chain, and when talks drift you have no agreed line to hold.

options.text: The $3M–$6M range, the reasons behind it, and a walk-away price set now
options.feedback: The board sees what drives the value and agrees a limit before emotions kick in. Talks can then move without moving your ceiling.

options.text: $7.2M, close to the broker's view, so you don't lose the deal
options.feedback: You'd likely win the deal. You'd also pay for safety the business doesn't have.

cards.title: Your valuation, step by step.

breakdown.label: Equipment
breakdown.detail: Needed every year to keep running

cards.softwareNote: The same chain works for buying a software company. Start from cash after the spending needed to keep the product alive, cut the multiple for churn or one giant customer, and compare payment terms in today's money.

cards.title: Every step was a judgment call.
body: Why 4.5 times and not 5? That's an opinion, and the seller will have a different one.
The 10% rate is your company's assumption, too. At 5%, the installments would be worth about $5.63M, more than paying cash now.
And installments are a loan from the seller. If the chain leaves, you still owe $1.3M every year. **Write down each assumption** so you know which one to revisit when facts change.

cards.title: A price is a chain of judgments. Write each one down.
body: Each call you made used one idea from this unit:
list: **Which number:** value the cash an owner gets, not headline profit
**Which multiple:** a multiple is shorthand for risk and growth, so adjust it
**How to pay:** money later is worth less, so compare offers in today's money
**What to show:** values swing with assumptions, so show a range and set a walk-away price
cards.callout: **Try it today:** for your own business, write down its yearly cash after needed spending, its biggest risk, and the multiple you'd accept as a buyer.
